headline: What Amy Poehler’s New Series, ‘Dig,’ Gets Right About Archaeology

paragraphs.text: A distinctive rubber bucket used for moving excavated dirt, known as a zembeli. A mass spectrometer needed for carbon dating ancient artifacts. And a laser theodolite, which helps map the coordinates of a dig site with extreme accuracy.

Such tools are more commonly found at archaeological excavations and laboratories than they are on sitcom sets, but they all feature in “Dig,” a new comedy series starring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie that is scheduled to premiere on Peacock on Nov. 23.

Getting the science — not to mention the history — right was crucial to creating the sets and dialogue for the show, which follows four researchers who make a once-in-a-lifetime discovery while digging near a fictional town in Greece.

Not included among those scientists is Joseph L. Rife, an anthropologist at Vanderbilt University who specializes in the ancient Mediterranean. But Dr. Rife played a different role in the production — archaeology consultant.

The show’s plot might be fictitious, but for the titular dig to come off as believable, it was Dr. Rife’s job to make sure the site and the science around it looked real (or at least real for a television show shot on the Universal Studios backlot).
In recreating the archaeological site at the center of the plot, “the nuts and bolts had to be accurate,” Dr. Rife said.

Getting those fundamentals right meant portraying the work of classical archaeology, the study of material artifacts related to the cultures of the ancient Mediterranean through excavation. (Think ancient Greece and Rome, but also related civilizations like the Etruscans and Minoans.)

Such archaeologists work to understand the complex cultures of ancient societies, including their religious beliefs, politics and economies. But unlike researchers studying some other parts of the ancient world or periods of prehistory, classical archaeologists are aided by an abundance of complementary sources — including art, architecture and literature that have survived millenniums.
“You not only excavate the buildings where assemblies met,” Dr. Rife said, “but you can also read the speeches they gave.”

Using known pieces of art and literature, archaeologists can determine where to dig, and they can date newly uncovered artifacts to fixed timelines. (Such techniques were instrumental in uncovering some of the region’s most famous sites, including Pompeii and Troy, as well as in excavating wonders like the Colosseum and the Parthenon.)

Dating objects along an established chronology through the use of art and epigraphy (the study of ancient inscriptions etched into hard surfaces like stone) is important to the show’s not-to-be-spoiled discovery. That moment, Dr. Rife said, was intended to mimic a “realistic archaeological discovery.”

Kate Myers, the author of the novel “Excavations” on which the show is based, said getting the objects right was important for the production because an appreciation of artifacts is central to archaeology.

“So much of working in archaeology is this deep respect for the objects and for the process of uncovering,” said Ms. Myers, who studied archaeology at the University of Pennsylvania, and whose own experience working on a dig inspired the book.
Verisimilitude, however, wasn’t just a matter of getting the artifacts right. Set designers also had to build sets that duplicated dig sites and laboratories.

“We got notes about what the soil would look like and how the trenches should be laid out,” said Dan Bishop, the production designer, who built the show’s sets. “We were able to model and draw plans for burning pits, stones for floors and the way walls are put together on a dig site. We spent a lot of time studying limestone.”
Small details mattered, including zembelis, rubber buckets made from recycled tires that are “emblematic” of dig sites across the Mediterranean.

On prominent display in scenes of the lab is a spectrometer, a machine that separates atoms by mass-to-charge ratio, allowing scientists to calculate the age of a sample based on the radioactive decay rates of certain isotopes.

And in the background of several other scenes, viewers can see a laser theodolite, a surveying tool that projects a visible laser used to map excavation grids and that can track the location and depth of artifacts.

For inspiration, Dr. Rife brought the show’s producers to working excavations in Greece, including to the southern village of Kenchreai, where the archaeologist has been conducting excavations since 2002. They also visited digs in the ancient cities of Isthmia, Sicyon and Epidaurus.
Most of what is discovered at a typical dig are mundane pieces of broken pottery — shards of pots, jugs and bowls that have been untouched by human hands for thousands of years.

It is these everyday objects that allow archaeologists to piece together the lives of people who would otherwise be forgotten. A discarded pot or the remains of a meal can reveal how people ate, worked and lived — and, collectively, tell a story that a single extraordinary artifact cannot.
Treasures, like the show’s plot-turning discovery, are rare. But archaeologists like Dr. Rife prefer it that way.
“I would be much more excited to excavate a garbage pit in an impoverished house than I would a piece of gold jewelry,” he said.
